vignette:
Martin is a 68-year-old married European American man who has worked for decades as a psychologist, a role that makes his current difficulties feel especially disorienting to him. When he speaks about the abuse, his account does not unfold as a steady story. Instead, it comes in sharply preserved stills: the angle of a hallway lamp, the pattern of fabric on a blouse, the sudden nearness of a bicycle wheel, his own body bracing before he fully understood what was happening. He says that when he tries to tell himself what happened, he cannot make it cohere from beginning to end. What comes most readily are photographs in his mind, disconnected but vivid, and at other times there is no picture at all, only a rush of the same terror and helplessness that overtakes him without warning.

The abuse occurred in the context of a romantic relationship in later life, something Martin still struggles to reconcile with the assumptions he once held about intimacy, maturity, and safety. He had believed that by his age he understood people well, perhaps better than most, and that the world, while imperfect, was still basically navigable if one paid attention. Those beliefs feel ruined to him now. He is left with the sense that people are not what they seem and that he himself failed in some essential way to recognize danger when it was close beside him. He has come to believe that this says something humiliating about him, that he is inadequate in ways he cannot easily name.

Certain details from the abuse now have a peculiar force in his everyday life. Bicycles are one of them. The sight of a bicycle on a sidewalk or locked outside a coffee shop can stop him internally before he knows why, as if one of those frozen images has been pulled forward into the present. Crowded places are another. In a tightly packed grocery aisle or a busy lobby, the press of bodies and movement makes him feel exposed and keyed up. He scans faces and posture, following people with his eyes for signs that they might turn unpredictable or harmful. He knows how excessive this can look from the outside, but from his perspective vigilance feels necessary; he no longer assumes safety simply because a setting is ordinary.

Being alone with women has become especially difficult, and this has altered the texture of his work. As a psychologist, he is regularly in situations that involve privacy, emotional intensity, and one-to-one conversation. He notices himself tensing when he is scheduled to meet alone with a woman, monitoring every shift in tone and movement, watching closely in a way that leaves him drained rather than professionally engaged. The problem is not abstract. It appears in the consulting room, in doorways, in moments before a session begins. He feels ashamed of this, both because it constricts his practice and because it clashes with how he understands himself.

Over the months after the abuse, Martin developed small, rigid habits meant to keep himself steady. He avoids wearing clothes that resemble what he had on during the abuse, changing shirts if something about the cut or color feels too close to one of those mental snapshots. He works hard to control his emotions and speaks of this almost as a duty. What he is most determined not to feel is anger. He never allows himself to express it and scarcely permits himself to recognize it internally. He presents as measured and composed, but the effort is constant. His wife has noticed how tightly managed he has become, how quickly he redirects conversations that come near the relationship or the abuse, and how much of him seems occupied by holding something in place.

Nights are particularly revealing of how unsafe he feels. He wakes and checks his surroundings to confirm that he is safe, sometimes more than once. Darkness feels less trustworthy than daylight; at night he is more alert to sounds, more inclined to listen and assess, less able to settle fully into sleep. Even when there is no image in mind, he can be seized by the emotional intensity of the event, as though his body has recognized danger ahead of his thoughts.

What finally brought Martin to seek help was not a single crisis but the accumulation of these changes in a life that had once felt solid. He could see his world narrowing: the places he was reluctant to go, the carefulness around clothing, the altered stance in his office, the strain on closeness at home. More than anything, he was frightened by how completely his basic trust had been damaged. He wants help because he no longer wants to live as if harm could emerge from any crowded room, any bicycle passing by, or any private interaction with a woman. At the same time, what frightens him most is the possibility that the abuse revealed something permanent—about the world, about other people, and about himself—that cannot be repaired.
